title: PingFederate ID-JAG: grant
lede: Imported flow from the pf Id Jag diagram.

nodes.label: User + agent
sub: browser holds a session cookie only

nodes.label: MCP Authorization Server
sub: oauth-mcp · mints its own access token

steps.title: Start the UC40 MCP request
steps.what: The BFF receives the user's request and keeps OAuth tokens out of the browser. The UC40 PingFederate lane uses its server-held refresh token as the upstream subject.
steps.why: The browser never holds a token, so there is nothing for page script to steal.

steps.title: Side 1 · PingFederate validates the upstream token
steps.what: The BFF sends a token-exchange request with the refresh token, its token type, the downstream audience/resource, and requested scopes. PingFederate's token-exchange policy validates the refresh token.
steps.why: The exchange runs as the same client that received the refresh token; PingFederate binds refresh tokens to their client.

steps.title: PingFederate mints the ID-JAG
steps.what: After validation and attribute mapping, PingFederate builds and signs the ID-JAG. Its audience identifies the downstream authorization server; its resource and scope constrain the MCP access being requested.
steps.why: The assertion is audience-bound: only the named authorization server can use it.

steps.title: PingFederate issues the ID-JAG
steps.what: PingFederate returns a signed ID-JAG to the BFF in access_token, with issued_token_type naming it an ID-JAG. The BFF refuses the wrong type, issuer, audience or expiry before using it.
steps.why: Checking on receipt means a misconfigured exchange fails here, not three hops later.

steps.title: Side 2 · submit ID-JAG for validation
steps.what: The BFF sends the ID-JAG to the configured downstream MCP authorization server as a JWT bearer assertion. The MCP AS checks issuer/signature, audience, expiry, ID-JAG type, its resource allowlist, and the single-use jti.
steps.why: A second server judges a credential the first server signed: that is cross-app access.

steps.title: Downstream AS issues its local access token
steps.what: A successful JWT bearer grant returns a resource-specific MCP access token. The ID-JAG was the grant assertion; the newly issued access token is what authorizes the protected call.
steps.why: The ID-JAG is spent here and goes no further.

steps.title: Call the protected MCP tool
steps.what: The BFF sends the MCP request to PingGateway with the downstream access token.
steps.why: PingGateway enforces the token before the MCP server sees the call.

steps.title: PingGateway asks PingOne Authorize
steps.what: PingGateway asks PingOne Authorize for the action-policy decision before the MCP server is allowed to run the tool.
steps.why: A valid token is not enough: policy decides the action.

steps.title: The permitted call reaches the MCP server
steps.what: After PERMIT, PingGateway forwards the same access token to the MCP server (the OLB backend) that owns get_my_accounts.
steps.why: The token is passed along unchanged because its audience already matches.

steps.title: The MCP server reads the data
steps.what: The MCP server passes the same access token to the BFF banking API. The banking API verifies the signature and exact issuer, applies audience, scope and role checks, and returns the data. The ID-JAG never reaches this hop.
steps.why: Every hop after Side 2 sees only the access token.
